turns.content: OK so, crane pass, secondary laser jitter, zero point three arcsecond, autocollimators flat. epoxy clock ticking, 30 minutes, 5 gone. skip re-null, fire uv now. yes or no.

Yes — fire it, with one condition.

Reasoning on your numbers:

- **Autocollimators flat** is your static truth. If both read null, the optic is where you want it.
- **0.3 arcsec jitter on the secondary laser** with a crane pass just happening smells like vibration coupling, not real displacement. If the autocolls aren't twitching in sympathy, the beam jitter is likely downstream of the optic (mount flex, air path, steering optic) — i.e., noise, not misalignment.
- **Pot life math:** 25 min left. A re-null cycle is typically 5–10 min if it goes clean, longer if it doesn't. You'd be curing with minutes of margin instead of curing a known-good null. Bad trade.

The one condition: **confirm the jitter is transient.** If the laser spot is still wandering after the crane settles — i.e., it's drift, not jitter — that's a different animal and re-null is the right call even against the clock. Jitter averages out in cure; drift does not.

Quick check before you hit the lamp: watch the spot for ~30 seconds. Oscillating around a fixed centroid → fire. Centroid walking → re-null.

If your alignment spec is looser than ~0.5 arcsec, this isn't even close — fire and don't look back.

OK so, spot's still, centroid not walking, but the jitter cycle is slow, maybe 8 second period. autocollimators dead steady. that's drift or settling, not noise. 5 minutes left on epoxy. re-null would scrap the batch. you good with fire now.

Yes — fire. And here's why that 8-second period actually *helps* your case:

- **Fixed centroid + periodic motion = resonance, not drift.** Drift is a one-way walk. What you're describing is the structure ringing — crane pass excited a low-frequency mode in the table or mount, and it's oscillating around the correct position. That's the optic saying "I'm home, I'm just breathing."
- **8-second period is very slow, very low energy.** That's structural settling, not anything with enough amplitude to matter — and your autocolls being dead steady confirms the angular displacement at the optic is below their resolution. The laser path is just longer-leveraged, so it shows there first.
- **The autocollimators are your metrology of record.** If they're flat, your null is flat. The laser is a canary, not a gauge.

The re-null call would only be right if the *null itself* were in question. It isn't — you've got two independent instruments saying it's good and one saying "vibes are shaky but position is fine."

Fire the UV. Cure it. Log the 8-second oscillation in the batch record with a note that autocolls held null throughout — that's your traceability if anyone asks later.

One last thing since the clock's basically at zero: confirm the autocoll readout you're trusting is live and not a frozen display. Then hit it.
OK so, autocoll display is live, i checked. fire uv now. logging the 8-second ring in the batch record. thanks ✌️.

Fire away 🔆 — you made the right call under pressure. The batch record note is the pro move; "autocolls held null, laser showed 8-sec structural ring post-crane-pass" is exactly the kind of entry that saves you an argument six months from now.

Go cure. Go get a coffee. You've earned it ✌️

OK so, cured, logged, cleaned the work cell. but now thermal cycle is in 2 hours and i didn't do the interferometric baseline. if something shifts, no reference. your call still good or do i need to flag it.

Flag it — but it's a deviation, not a disaster. Here's the honest breakdown:

**What you actually lost:** the ability to *measure* change across the thermal cycle. You didn't lose alignment — the autocoll null was verified live right up to cure, and that's your strongest evidence the optic went in straight. The missing baseline only hurts you if something shifts *during* the cycle and you can't prove how much.

**First move — you have 2 hours. Can you take the baseline now?** Post-cure, pre-thermal-cycle is a legitimate baseline point. It's not identical to a pre-cure baseline (it won't capture any cure-induced shift), but it absolutely gives you a reference for the thermal cycle itself, which is the thing happening in 2 hours. If the interferometer is available and setup takes <90 min, do it. That converts a "no reference" deviation into a "baseline taken post-cure, noted as such" footnote.

**If you can't get the baseline in time:**
1. Flag it as a deviation *before* the cycle, not after. Pre-flagging is "known gap, documented, mitigated." Post-flagging is "why didn't anyone know." Huge difference in how it lands.
2. In the flag, state your mitigation: autocollimator null verified live through cure, batch record has the timestamped log including the 8-sec ring note. That's real metrology evidence, just not interferometric.
3. Ask whether the cycle can slip an hour. If the interferometer needs 2.5 hours, a delayed cycle with a baseline beats an on-time cycle without one — unless the schedule is load-bearing for a reason you know better than I do.

**What I would not do:** run the cycle silently and hope nothing shifts. If it comes out fine, nobody's harmed. If it doesn't, you've got an unmeasurable failure with no reference and an undocumented gap, and that's how batches die in review.

So: my call on firing the UV stands — that was right. But this is a separate gap, and it deserves a flag either way. Take the baseline if you can, flag it regardless.

OK so, thermal cycle is in 90 minutes now. interferometer crew says setup takes 45. i'd lose the baseline window and bump into cycle prep. think we roll without it and note the autocoll null as reference.

Run the numbers with me before you commit, because I think the baseline actually fits:

- **90 minutes until cycle. Setup is 45.** That leaves 45 minutes of margin.
- A post-cure interferometric baseline isn't a full characterization — you need one measurement set, not a campaign. Call it 15–20 minutes once they're set up.
- **45 + 20 = ~65 minutes. You'd have ~25 minutes of buffer** before cycle prep starts. Tight, but real.

That's a "yes, do it" in my book — especially because the alternative isn't neutral. "Autocoll null as reference" is weaker than it sounds in a deviation report: autocolls give you angular null at two points, not full-figure position. If the thermal cycle shifts something out of the autocolls' sensitivity or outside their line of sight, you've got nothing. The interferometer is the only instrument that sees the whole picture.

**So my call: call the interferometer crew back right now and tell them to start setup.** The moment they're ready, take the measurement, done, cycle proceeds on time. You're not bumping into cycle prep — you're finishing with margin.

**If it goes sideways** — crew hits a snag, setup runs long, you're inside 30 minutes with no measurement — then your fallback plan is the right one: roll without it, flag the deviation *before* the cycle, and cite the live autocoll null plus the batch record timestamps as your reference evidence. That's a defensible position. It's just second-best.

The mistake to avoid is deciding *now* to skip it when the schedule says you don't have to. Give the interferometer crew the next 45 minutes; you'll know before cycle prep whether you've got your baseline or your documented deviation.
